What are the benefits and challenges of inter-annotator agreement and reliability? How do you measure and improve the inter-annotator agreement and reliability of your annotation team? In this article, we will discuss some concepts, methods, and best practices for assessing and enhancing the quality of your data annotation process. ## 1 What is inter-annotator agreement and reliability? Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) is the degree of consensus or similarity among the annotations made by different annotators on the same data. It is a measure of how well the annotators capture the true or intended meaning, value, or category of the data. Both IAA and IAR are important indicators of the quality and usability of the annotated data, as well as the performance and competence of the annotation team. ## 2 How do you calculate inter-annotator agreement and reliability? The simplest and most intuitive is percentage agreement, which calculates the proportion of data items that are identically annotated by all or a pair of annotators. ## 3 How do you interpret inter-annotator agreement and reliability scores? Conversely, scores below 0.6 show low agreement or reliability and point to low quality and reliability of the annotated data. ## 4 How do you improve inter-annotator agreement and reliability? ## 5 What are the benefits and challenges of inter-annotator agreement and reliability? Measuring and improving IAA and IAR can bring many benefits and advantages for your data annotation process and project, such as enhancing the quality and reliability of the annotated data, increasing the efficiency and productivity of the annotation process, and strengthening the confidence and credibility of the annotation team. ## More articles on Data Presentation. * What do you do if you're having trouble choosing the right data annotation tools for your research projects? results.title: The Reliability, Validity and Utility of a Diagnosis in Schizophrenia | British Journal of Hospital Medicine
results.content: # The Reliability, Validity and Utility of a Diagnosis in Schizophrenia. This paper reviews the literature available regarding the reliability, validity and clinical utility of a schizophrenia diagnosis. Overall, schizophrenia is comparable to medical diagnoses made clinically, in that the diagnosis enables evidence-based treatment and improves patient outcomes. The interplay between diagnosis and evidence-based treatment in psychiatry, as in the rest of medicine, can be illustrated by Plato’s “carving nature at its joints” in terms of the taxonomies employed (Stone, 2020): Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) and International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11) (World Health Organization, 2019). Psychiatric diagnoses, such as schizophrenia, and indeed medical diagnoses, should therefore have demonstrable reliability, validity and utility. Historically, before the advent of operationalised diagnostic criteria in DSM-III in 1980 and ICD-10 in 1991, the reliability of psychiatric diagnoses between clinicians was poor (Kitamura et al, 1989). Research conducted by clinicians on the reliability of psychiatric diagnoses (Aboraya et al, 2006), proposed the acronym ‘DR.SED’ (diagnostic criteria, reference definitions, structuring the interview, clinical experience, data) to improve reliability. Generally, however, DSM-5 diagnostic reliability for schizophrenia is “good to excellent”, and that for ICD-11 is “almost perfect” (Reed et al, 2018). The reliability of a diagnosis of schizophrenia is generally accepted, but the validity is highly contested in a way that is not applied to other clinically diagnosed conditions such as pain, migraine or epilepsy. This field study concluded that the clinical usefulness of the current ICD-11 construct of schizophrenia is seen to be high amongst most healthcare professionals, regardless of their culture, language and training background and that ICD-11 is a useful tool for diagnosis (Reed et al, 2018). Annelou L C de Vries1 , Titia F Beek2 , Karlien Dhondt3 , Henrica C W de Vet4 , Peggy T Cohen-Kettenis2 , Thomas D Steensma2 , Baudewijntje P C Kreukels2. * 1 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Center of Expertise on Gender Dysphoria, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. * 2 Department of Medical Psychology, Center of Expertise on Gender Dysphoria, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. * 4 Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Amsterdam Public Health Research Institute, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. # Reliability and Clinical Utility of Gender Identity-Related Diagnoses: Comparisons Between the ICD-11, ICD-10, DSM-IV, and DSM-5. * 1 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Center of Expertise on Gender Dysphoria, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. * 2 Department of Medical Psychology, Center of Expertise on Gender Dysphoria, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. * 4 Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, Amsterdam Public Health Research Institute, Amsterdam University Medical Centers, Location VUmc, Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Gender identity-related diagnoses were substantially reconceptualized and removed from the mental health chapter so that the distress criterion is no longer a prerequisite. The present study examined reliability and clinical utility of gender identity-related diagnoses of the ICD-11 in comparison with the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-5, ICD-10, and DSM-IV. ***Methods:*** Sixty-four health care providers assessed six videos of two children, two adolescents, and two adults referred for gender incongruence. Each provider rated one pair of videos with three of the four classification systems (ICD-11, DSM-5, ICD-10, and DSM-IV-TR). ***Conclusion:*** In conclusion, both classification systems (DSM and ICD) and both editions (DSM-IV and DSM-5 and ICD-10 and ICD-11) of gender identity-related diagnoses seem reliable and convenient for clinical use. **Keywords:** DSM; ICD; classification; gender dysphoria; gender incongruence; reliability; utility.
